items.title: Signing & packing state
items.description: Establish how much trust the OS places in this binary and whether it has been tampered with. Confirm Authenticode/catalog signing, inspect section entropy for packing or overlay data, and note that a signed, trusted LOLBIN raises the impact of every other finding here.
items.examples:
rabin2 -I samples/setx.exe
r2 -q -c 'iI~signed' samples/setx.exe   # embedded Authenticode; catalog-signed system files show 'false'
r2 -q -c 'iS entropy' samples/setx.exe   # high-entropy sections hint at packing

items.title: Stack/heap buffer overflow
items.description: Trace every copy of attacker-controlled input (argv, file contents, registry values) into fixed-size buffers. Look for copies with no length bound or a bound derived from the source instead of the destination. Decompile the handling function and confirm the destination size.
items.examples:
r2 -q -c 'aaa;afl~sym' samples/setx.exe   # locate parsing/handler functions
PyGhidra: decompile the arg-parser and any Reg*/file-read handler, check destination buffer sizes
Grep decompiled C for stack arrays written in a loop with no bound

items.title: Integer overflow in size/offset math
items.description: Find arithmetic on lengths, counts or offsets that feeds an allocation, copy length or array index. Attacker-controlled offsets/lengths (e.g. setx /A x,y,x1,y2 coordinates) that are added or multiplied without overflow/range checks can wrap and cause out-of-bounds reads or writes.
items.examples:
Decompile the offset/length parser and follow each value into malloc/memcpy/index math
Craft an input with a huge or negative offset and trace whether it is range-checked
r2: comment the size computation and audit the bounds test before the copy

items.title: Unsafe C runtime / string APIs
items.description: Enumerate imports and internal calls for classically unsafe APIs (strcpy, strcat, sprintf, gets, scanf, memcpy with attacker length, system/_wsystem, CreateProcess with unquoted paths). For each hit, confirm whether attacker input actually reaches it.
items.examples:
rabin2 -i samples/setx.exe   # import table
r2 -q -c 'aaa;axt @ sym.imp.strcpy' samples/setx.exe   # callers of an unsafe API
capa -vv samples/setx.exe > work/capa_verbose.txt

items.title: DLL search-order hijacking
items.description: Review static and delay-load imports and any explicit LoadLibrary/LoadLibraryEx calls for DLLs loaded by name without a fully-qualified path. Such loads are hijackable when the binary runs from a writable or attacker-controlled working directory.
items.examples:
rabin2 -i samples/setx.exe | grep -i delay   # delay-load stubs (e.g. WNetAddConnection2W)
r2 -q -c 'aaa;axt @ sym.imp.LoadLibraryW' samples/setx.exe
List imported DLLs and check which resolve by bare name vs absolute path

items.title: Arbitrary file-read primitive
items.description: Determine whether the binary can be coerced into reading a file the caller should not be able to read and surfacing its contents (into an env var, output, or registry value). setx /F reading an arbitrary file is the archetype. Prove exactly what content ends up observable and where.
items.examples:
Decompile the /F file-read handler and trace where the bytes are stored
Point /F at a file outside the expected location and observe the resulting env var value
Document a concrete command line and the disclosed content

items.title: Registry read/write abuse
items.description: Analyse how the binary parses and accesses registry paths (e.g. setx /K reg:key, and the HKCU/HKLM write it performs). Check whether the key path can point somewhere it shouldn't, whether HKLM keys can be reached, and whether this yields a read/write primitive or a persistence mechanism.
items.examples:
Decompile the /K registry-source handler and the value-write path
Test whether /K reg:key can reference an HKLM key the tool shouldn't expose
Chain a crafted value into a registry write to build an indirect-persistence PoC

items.title: Indirect value sourcing (command-line-log evasion)
items.description: Establish which of {variable name, target key path, value} must be typed literally on the command line versus sourced indirectly from a file or registry. Anything sourced indirectly evades command-line logging/telemetry (Sysmon EID 1, EDR) and is the core LOLBAS abuse angle for this binary.
items.examples:
Trace /F, /A, /R, /X and /K to see which fields can come from a file/registry instead of argv
Build a command line where the sensitive value never appears in the process command line
Document what a defender relying on command-line logging would miss

items.title: Undocumented switches / dead code
items.description: Compare the full function/branch inventory against the documented usage text. Flag branches only reachable via a comparison to a constant string not in the help output, functions with no xrefs (dead or indirectly-called code), and anything that looks like a leftover test hook, debug flag or Easter egg.
items.examples:
r2 -q -c 'aaa;afl' samples/setx.exe   # total functions vs the ones reachable from documented switches
r2 -q -c 'axt @ fcn.NNNN' samples/setx.exe   # callers of a function with no obvious entry
Diff string-compared switch tokens against the /? usage text

items.title: Format-string usage
items.description: Look for printf-family calls whose format argument is (or can be influenced by) attacker input rather than a literal. A user-controlled format string enables memory disclosure or, in some cases, writes.
items.examples:
r2 -q -c 'aaa;axt @ sym.imp.printf' samples/setx.exe   # and wprintf/sprintf/_snwprintf
Decompile each caller and confirm the format argument is a constant literal
Flag any call where argv/file/registry data reaches the format position

items.title: Argument validation & bounds
items.description: For this specific switch / value-source mechanism, decompile its handler and audit how it validates and bounds its arguments. Feed over-long, empty, malformed and boundary-value inputs and confirm each is checked before use in copies, allocations or indexing.
items.examples:
PyGhidra: decompile this switch's handler function
Craft over-long and empty argument values and trace the validation path in r2
Record which inputs are rejected vs silently accepted

items.title: Offset/length parsing safety
items.description: Where this switch parses numeric offsets or lengths (e.g. /A x,y,x1,y2 coordinates, /R regex ranges), test for integer overflow, negative values and out-of-bounds reads. Confirm the parsed numbers are range-checked against the actual source-data size before use.
items.examples:
Supply huge, zero and negative offsets and trace the size math in the decompiler
Check whether the offset is validated against the length of the /F source file
Look for wraparound turning a large offset into a small/negative index

items.title: Indirect sourcing via this switch
items.description: Determine whether this switch lets the variable name, key path or value be supplied from a file or registry rather than typed literally, so it never appears in the process command line. If so, document a concrete working command line demonstrating the command-line-logging evasion.
items.examples:
Test whether this switch's value can come from /F <file> or /K reg:key instead of argv
Run it and confirm the sensitive data is absent from the process command line
Write up the exact PoC command line and what a defender would and wouldn't see

items.title: File/registry disclosure via this switch
items.description: Test whether this switch can be pointed at a file or registry key the caller shouldn't be able to read and have its contents surface (in an env var, output or written value). Prove the disclosure with a concrete target and capture the leaked content.
items.examples:
Point this switch at a sensitive file/key outside its intended location
Observe whether the resulting env var / output reveals the content
Capture the command line and the disclosed data as evidence
